At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities.
  • Industry observers note that more than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay.
  • Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.” Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch.

Industry observers note that more than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”.

Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.

Industry observers note that the work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas mentioned. “So is the past present or is the present past?”.

The Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”.

Industry observers note that consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.

It has been revealed that for Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he said.

Industry observers note that histories of state-sanctioned violence and resistance movements similarly converge across a nearly eleven-foot-wide canvas in Mickalene Thomas’s 2021 mixed-media painting The Charnel House (Resist #5). Reworking Picasso’s 1944–45 masterpiece of corpses heaped beneath a table made in response to news footage of liberated Nazi concentration camps, Thomas collages photographs and placards from the Civil Rights and Black Lives Matter movements with the modernist’s fragmented anatomical forms. A poster advertising the Black Panther Party’s free breakfast program appears beside a portrait of Angela Davis and the names of Freddie Gray and Alton Sterling, both killed during encounters with police. Here, grief and trauma are paired with resistance and community building.

The language of dissent assumes a subtler register in Ligon’s Narratives (1993), a suite of nine sepia-toned etchings that mimic the ornate typography and florid prose of 19th-century slave narratives. Ligon replaces accounts of enslavement and escape with details from his early education at a predominantly white private school, his desire for other men, and the circumstances of his career as an artist. In his hands, a literary form that freed Black people used to demonstrate their humanity becomes a medium for contemporary self-portraiture and self-determination.

According to recent reports, museums, of course, too, play a role in shaping public records. Over the past five years, the Broad has acquired work by 26 artists previously unrepresented in its collection, many of whom are of a younger generation and, like Rosales, actively working in LA. Heyler sees these acquisitions as part of an ongoing effort to better reflect the multiplicity of the communities that surround the institution. “We’re not telling one story but many,” she mentioned. “We’re always striving to strengthen the connective tissues between them.”.

The exhibition offers an opportunity to showcase many of the newly acquired artists and to extend an art-historical conversation that Heyler traces to exhibitions like “A Forest of Signs: Art in the Crisis of Representation,” a landmark 1989 survey at the Museum of Contemporary Art, just across the street. Bringing together works by 30 American artists, from Jeff Koons to Jenny Holzer, that show examined the unstable boundaries between reality and representation in an increasingly media-saturated society. But the terrain has evolved, Heyler noted. Where artists of that period often exposed the ideologies concealed by authoritative and commercial imagery, audiences today, immersed in social media and generative AI, navigate what she called a “stew of falsehoods and truths.”.

It has been revealed that even so, curator Vanegas Rocha hopes her exhibition inspires something more generative than cynicism, in which artists can be seen as the “architects of better futures.” She locates the potential for systemic change in the power of an individual aesthetic encounter. “It can teach you about the world, about others, about yourself,” she noted. “That single moment can have a ripple effect, leading to a collective difference.” Rosales, likewise, hasn’t relinquished hope. Citing José Esteban Muñoz’s 2009 queer theory book Cruising Utopia, she described hope as an ever-receding horizon that we must continue to endeavor toward. “We are a people that don’t give up,” she said, noting that her mother also took her to protests from an early age. “Standing up for each other, even when you don’t see it right away, does pay off.” Progress, she suggests, may not be linear or inevitable, but that doesn’t make it an illusion. In her mirror, the unresolved question—“Has the Myth Been Shattered?”—is cast back onto the people who might yet determine the answer.

Industry News: Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that barefoot walks on the beach.
  • Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not new, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—substantial and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not new, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

In a recent development, for some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

It has been revealed that “It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” says Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting new collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” notes Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

Industry observers note that this type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” claims Dr. Pearl.

It has been revealed that dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

It has been revealed that try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

But will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” indicates Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

In a recent development, if you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

If injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a proposal to minimize your pain.

Lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.

Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign, which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is currently exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society,” mentioned Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.” Related Articles Artist Tracey Rose Accuses Swiss Museum of Censoring Video Referring to 'Muslim Holocaust' Art Recovered in $400,000 Colorado Theft, Portland Museum Picks Architects for $100 M. Expansion, and More: Morning Links for January 10, 2023.

In a recent development, schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the umbrella foundation of Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee, stated in a statement that Schmidt brings “remarkable professional expertise, international experience and a deep understanding of people” as she shapes the next “development phase of our museums.”.

Industry observers note that before joining Brücke-Museum, Schmidt was a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and a curator at the Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. She studied art history and modern German literature in Marburg, Amsterdam, and Berlin before graduating from the Royal College of Art.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million) at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).
  • Recent findings suggest that legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts.
  • Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million) at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Recent findings suggest that legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “jatte-téton” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape. Related Articles Auction of Nazi-Looted Torah Fragment Canceled After Outcry and Israeli Government Intervention Can AI Help Identify the Sitters in Historical Portraits?

Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.

Sources indicate that three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.

Recent findings suggest that with the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.

Speaking to Le Journal des Arts about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”.

#217628. Tech Report: What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1191 w)

Tech Report: What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one issue keeps coming up: the side effects.
  • To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet.
  • But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one issue keeps coming up: the side effects. As notable as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she states. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”.

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen notes.

Recent findings suggest that you can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen claims. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

It has been revealed that fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing concern worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen indicates: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

According to recent reports, now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen states.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen states. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Recent findings suggest that then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

Recent findings suggest that people who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we noted above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen notes. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”.

It has been revealed that another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

According to recent reports, whatever upcoming fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

#217626. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1006 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • It has been revealed that that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a upcoming reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

It has been revealed that that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

It has been revealed that but is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a substantial deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

According to recent reports, beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Sources indicate that despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

In a recent development, studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial challenges that occur with age, Dr. Molina indicates. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson notes. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

It has been revealed that there’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she notes—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

Recent findings suggest that one 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

Recent findings suggest that however, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

It has been revealed that the critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, Upcoming York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

In a recent development, the term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

It has been revealed that nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate proposal.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate strategy.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

According to recent reports, A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Industry observers note that without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

The living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate proposal is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing people with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.
  • Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.
  • Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing people with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly – its AI creative studio – through the Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta.

People can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.

Adobe has also released Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe mentioned the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.

The brand’s latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing “AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on”.

Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, stated the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.

“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” said Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”.

Industry observers note that the Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io. In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.

The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining “in the director’s chair”.

In Premiere, the agent now supports latest capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.

The integrations will let customers instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

According to recent reports, layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so users can “step in at any moment to refine the work by hand”. The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

If a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

According to recent reports, adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

A newly introduced initiative mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, “guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve”.

Consumers can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.

In Firefly Boards, the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction”.

Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting newly introduced files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away”.

Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.

Among the other additions are a gallery of ready-made, quick actions, visual boards, and node-bases workflows through Firefly Graph (beta), which lets consumers build repeatable workflows of their own.

Adobe’s examples include turning a video storyboard into a finished cut and, in Firefly Design, carrying a brand identity from initial concept through client review within a single design workspace.

To learn more about the updates, visit Adobe’s website.

  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Recent findings suggest that keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of significant butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal problems and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins indicates about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in newly introduced people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Recent findings suggest that coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins indicates, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy fresh medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

According to recent reports, it’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

It has been revealed that but retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

According to recent reports, mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next significant thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Industry observers note that retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” indicates Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”.

Sources indicate that the medication is presently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide customers lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

Sources indicate that “Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”.

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”.

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

In a recent development, but compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

It has been revealed that dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you proposal to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he notes.

Industry observers note that but, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

Recent findings suggest that “Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle blueprint focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more key, he points out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Sources indicate that going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

It has been revealed that light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Recent findings suggest that light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

It has been revealed that working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

Recent findings suggest that an occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

In a recent development, diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

In a recent development, once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

  • The London maker of Milan design week’s much-discussed inflatable coffee table has unveiled his debut furniture collection, which includes veiny wax chairs and a rug adorned with cattle tags.
  • Jabez Bartlett is a British production-turned-furniture designer who caused a stir during April’s Milan design week, where he demonstrated a pillowy PVC coffee table topped with an opalescent resin surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by George Darrell unless stated otherwise.

The London maker of Milan design week’s much-discussed inflatable coffee table has unveiled his debut furniture collection, which includes veiny wax chairs and a rug adorned with cattle tags.

Jabez Bartlett is a British production-turned-furniture designer who caused a stir during April’s Milan design week, where he demonstrated a pillowy PVC coffee table topped with an opalescent resin surface.

A circular version followed, and both pieces are part of The Freight Proportioned to the Groove, an exhibition of his debut furniture collection that opens today in Hackney, London.

Bartlett told Dezeen that he wanted to start creating furniture to experiment with materials that he has used to bring film sets to life on screen.

According to recent reports, “With set design, things don’t necessarily have to be practical,” said the Devon-born designer. “It’s all about how they look on camera. I wanted to play with this in a more material and physical world.”.

“There’s a lot of industrial materials we’ve always used that I think are incredibly beautiful,” he continued. “It’s interesting to use something heavy and practical in a luxury piece.”.

Bartlett’s collection includes a triptych of marbled dining chairs made from a mixture of microcrystalline and crude oil wax cast in plywood frames.

The pieces were informed by a Japanese games table owned by the designer, characterised by a gridded top.

“I had the idea to remake it as a giant candle, with a wick in each square,” he explained. The idea became three chunky chairs that resemble large candles, embellished with playful wicks.

Bartlett’s collection also features a trio of lighting pieces clad in stretchy latex skins.

The smallest is a ceramic table lamp with a bloated shade, while the other two are angular floor lamps supported by metal structures, one of which was on display at the southwest London gallery Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

Despite their industrial materials, Bartlett also considers his pieces as nods to the wilderness.

Industry observers note that “I started off wanting to make brutalist-folk furniture, and now I’m seeing it, I feel like I got there,” he said. “Memory and illusion play a significant part, and of course, growing up in Devon leaves an imprint of the natural and the ancient world on you.”.

Another of the collection’s pieces is a large diamond-patterned textile rug, overdyed and bleached, and embellished with metal tags normally used to identify cattle.

The tags hem the rug and were also embroidered into its fabric in decorative circles.

Also on display in the exhibition are a monolithic cast acrylic mirror, a glossy black plinth and column with protruding thorns and another floor lamp with a similarly spiky, elongated black body and a sandy leather shade.

The title of Bartlett’s exhibition refers to the final line of poet Emily Dickinson’s 19th-century poem, That Love is All There Is.

It has been revealed that the Freight Proportioned to the Groove is on display from 26 to 29 November at Tuscany Wharf, 4B Orsman Road, London N1 5QJ. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#217613. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance.
  • According to recent reports, creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

According to recent reports, creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a substantial-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Industry observers note that because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s vital to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

It has been revealed that the same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

According to recent reports, some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

In a recent development, beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

It has been revealed that thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health problems that go beyond your hairstyle.

Industry observers note that furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Recent findings suggest that creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.
